newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bankers disagree over reasons for dollar strength.
newsitem.headline: Bankers disagree over reasons for dollar strength.

text.p: Top international bankers attending a conference on Tuesday disagreed over the reasons for the dollar's recent climb, with only one saying nervousness about Europe's planned currency union had played a part.
U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers, steering clear of the debate over the causes for the dollar's strength, said it was difficult to pick just one reason for the move.
"It is difficult to assign a single factor to the foreign exchange moves," Summers said, adding "we regard the most key factor for the strong dollar to be the solid fundamentals at home."
Summers was speaking from the United States through a video link while the governors of the German, French and British central banks joined commercial bankers in a podium discussion in Frankfurt.
The conference, called Global 24, was designed to discuss European monetary union.

Speaking in Frankfurt as the U.S. dollar traded just below the 1.7500 marks per dollar level, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer offered the same explanation he has given for months about the rise of the dollar.
The move "is more or less a correction (from exaggerated levels in the spring of 1995) and not an indicator that there is a loss of confidence that the euro will be strong," he said.
Senior Bundesbank officials have for months said they were not worried by the dollar's levels, stressing that moves of a few pfennigs in either direction would not be cause for concern.

Similarly Rolf Breuer, chairman of Germany's largest bank Deutsche Bank, said that international currency markets had not slipped into excessive turbulence in the runup to the launch of a common European currency in January 1999.
Referring to steps taken by European countries to ready themselves for currency union, Breuer said "we have converged sooner and without the turbulence people had expected."

Even as EU states enter the final leg of the race to currency union, Breuer ruled out any massive shifts in currency relationships. "The markets do not expect any turbulence," he said, adding he was confident the markets would remain free of turbulence in the next 400 to 500 days.
Bank of England governor Eddie George disagreed, saying markets were accutely aware of the potential implications of currency union and were acting accordingly.
For example the strength of the U.K. currency, which is not likely to be traded in for the euro in 1999, is partly based on concerns about Europe's currency union, George said.
"There is no question foreign exchange markets are persuaded of the political will to move ahead (on currency union)," George said, adding however "but the core (nations' currencies) are affected."
"The core strength of sterling is affected by this although there is a cyclical element (to the strength) as well," George added.

While some foreign exchange market participants have said the dollar has benefited from some sort of flight to quality out of the European currencies before currency union, Summers said the dollar had earned its current strength.
He said the dollar is not the default currency but rather thrives as a reflection of the strong U.S. economy, high level growth rates and low levels of inflation.
